name: Marion Tinsley
one_line: Over forty-five years and thousands of games, the best checkers player who ever lived lost seven of them.

facts.claim: lost seven games in the forty-five years from 1950 until his death in 1995, across thousands of tournament, championship, match, exhibition and casual games
facts.note: DISPUTED. Jonathan Schaeffer, Chinook's lead programmer, writes in Games of No Chance (MSRI Vol 29, 1996): 'Over the last forty-five years of his life ... Tinsley lost the unbelievable number of seven games.' Wikipedia agrees at seven. But the New York Times obituary of 8 April 1995 says he 'had lost only nine checkers games since first winning the world championship in 1955' - a HIGHER count over a SHORTER window, so the two cannot be reconciled as different measuring periods. Schaeffer's 2015 blog post hedges to 'lost less than 10'. Script must attribute: 'by most counts' or 'per the Chinook team'.

facts.claim: the count runs from an accidental loss in the 1950 U.S. Championship; after that he finished undivided first in every tournament he entered except his last
facts.note: The exception is the 1994 U.S. Championship, where he tied for first with Chinook and Don Lafferty.

facts.claim: contested nine World Championship matches and won every one, never losing a world championship match
facts.note: Schaeffer: 'He contested nine World Championship matches, winning each usually by an embarrassingly large margin.' Wikipedia independently confirms he never lost a world championship match.
The gap is not a decline - he retired from the game for twelve years for lack of competition, per Schaeffer.

facts.claim: beat the Chinook program 4 wins to 2 with 33 draws in the 1992 London Man-Machine match; those two were only his sixth and seventh losses since 1950
facts.note: August 1992, London, sponsored by Silicon Graphics, 40 games. Schaeffer: 'These were only the sixth and and seventh losses by Tinsley since 1950.' Note this was NOT the sanctioned World Championship - the ACF and EDA refused to sanction a computer challenger, so Tinsley resigned the title in 1992 in order to play, and was given the title World Champion Emeritus.

facts.claim: in the earlier 1990 exhibition he beat Chinook over fourteen games, winning 1-0 with thirteen draws
facts.note: This is the match containing the 'you're going to regret that' game. It is a fourteen-game exhibition in 1990, NOT the 1992 London championship - sources routinely conflate the two.

facts.claim: Chinook would have needed to search sixty moves deep to see that its tenth move in that game was already lost
facts.note: DISPUTED. Schaeffer's own paper says sixty: 'Chinook needed to look ahead sixty moves to know that its tenth move was a loser.' Wikipedia says Tinsley saw 'the win 64 moves into the future'. Prefer Schaeffer's sixty - he wrote the program and the paper - and attribute if used.

facts.claim: at that moment Chinook was searching twenty moves deep and reporting it had the advantage
facts.note: Schaeffer, firsthand: 'I sat there silent, thinking: What do you know? My program is searching twenty moves deep and says it has an advantage.'

facts.claim: Tinsley had seen to the end of the game and knew he had won at move eleven - one move after Chinook's mistake
facts.note: Schaeffer: 'In his notes to the game, Tinsley revealed that he had seen to the end of the game and knew he was going to win on move 11, one move after our mistake.'

facts.claim: opponents simply stopped playing him to win - for forty-five years most played only for the draw
facts.note: Schaeffer: 'For forty-five years, most of his opponents would play for the draw; going for a win was unthinkable.'

facts.claim: withdrew from the 1994 Man-Machine title match after six straight draws citing health; diagnosed with cancer a week later and died seven months after that, on 3 April 1995, aged 68
facts.note: Schaeffer confirms the sequence. Wikipedia specifies pancreatic cancer. He was a mathematics professor with a doctorate in combinatorial analysis from Ohio State.

facts.claim: his loss rate works out to roughly one game every six years (7 losses / 45 years = one per ~6.4 years)
facts.note: DERIVED, not quoted: straight arithmetic on Schaeffer's two sourced numbers (seven losses, forty-five years). Script should hedge with 'roughly' since 45/7 = 6.4.

facts.claim: no comparable figure exists in competitive mind games; the closest is Emanuel Lasker, chess world champion for over twenty years
facts.note: Schaeffer: 'Being the best over a 45-year period is unprecedented.' This is why comparison_type is streak and not gap - there is no clean numeric second-best in checkers to put on a card.

comparison.gap_description: Seven losses across forty-five years and thousands of games, from 1950 until his death.

story_beat: In 1990, playing the tenth game of a fourteen-game exhibition against the Chinook program, its programmer Jonathan Schaeffer reached out and played Chinook's tenth move; Tinsley looked up in surprise and said 'You're going to regret that.' Schaeffer sat there thinking his program was searching twenty moves deep and reporting an advantage - but Chinook's assessment slid from winning to equal to lost, and it eventually resigned.
